title: 2026-09-17 Justice Committee
machineSummary: Lisa Pizzoni of the Indigenous Data Authority and Craig Atkinson said the gang-funding prohibition bill lacks evidence and risks harming community providers. The sponsor said the bill targets $2.75 million-style funding to gang-affiliated entities like Kahukura, debating whether to narrow the definition from "associated" to "affiliated".

chunks.text: We've got you down for 10 minutes. If you can just leave some time at the end for questions. No problem at all. Over to you. Kia ora koutou. Ko Lisa Pizzoni toku ingoa. I'm the founder and lead architect of the Indigenous Data Authority, and I'm here in support of my written submission. I won't repeat the submission today, but I do want to focus on three things: the evidence for this bill, the distinction between association and wrongdoing, and the impact this legislation may have on Māori communities and providers.

I want to start by being very clear. I do not support public money being used to fund criminal activity or deliberately benefiting gangs. But before Parliament creates new legal obligations and criminal liability, I think it needs to clearly establish the problem it is trying to solve. The explanatory material tells us there is concern that public money could end up in the hands of gangs.

My question is, where is the evidence showing the scale of that problem? How often has it actually happened, and how much public money has been actually diverted? What existing safeguards have failed, and what evidence shows that this legislative response is necessary and proportionate? These are important questions when consequence of getting it wrong may include criminal liability.

If Kahukura is part of the justification for this concern, then I think we also need to look at the whole story. The Auditor-General examined that funding decision and found that the funding process had been followed. The application went through the required assessment process, and the contract contained controls for governance, monitoring, reporting, and audit.

The Auditor-General also found no evidence that the political views of H2R's co-director influenced the funding decision. So simply pointing to a gang connection does not establish that public money was misused. And that brings me to what I think is one of the most important principles here. Association may justify scrutiny. It does not establish wrongdoing.

We understand that principle elsewhere. We do not automatically conclude that a political donation proves improper influence. We do not automatically conclude that a relationship with a decision-maker proves corruption. And when we look at who may benefit from legislation progressed through processes such as fast track, association can raise legitimate questions, but questions still require evidence.

The same standard should apply here. Association is not evidence of misuse, connection is not evidence of diversion, and concern is not, by itself, an evidential basis for criminal liability. If association is enough to trigger scrutiny in one context, it cannot suddenly become proof in another.

And that is also why I referred to churches and faith-based institutes in my written submission. I want to be very clear. I'm not saying churches are gangs. I'm talking about consistency. The Royal Commission into Abuse and Care documented serious and widespread abuse within state and faith-based institutions, including institutional failures and failures of accountability. Some of that conduct was criminal, yet we do not say that every organization connected to a church should therefore be treated as suspect or excluded from

public funding. Nor should we. We look at who was responsible, we look at conduct, we look at control, and we look at the evidence. I'm simply asking Parliament to apply the same evidential principle here, because this bill will not operate in a vacuum. Māori are disproportionately represented in the criminal justice system and in gang-related settings, and that means the consequences of this legislation are likely to fall disproportionately within Māori communities and on organizations working directly with those whānau.

There is a fundamental difference between an organization being controlled by a gang and an organization working with people who have gang affiliations. And they're not the same thing. If the law does not make that distinction clearly enough, government agencies will need to manage the risk, and sometimes the easiest way to manage that risk is simply don't fund it.

That is the chilling effect I'm concerned about because the organizations affected may not be supporting criminal activity at all. They may be trying to reduce it. The New Zealand Law Society has also raised concerns about the workability of this bill, including uncertainty around who could potentially be criminally liable and how far the due diligence obligations extend.

If Parliament is going to create criminal liability, people should not have to guess where that liability begins and ends. So my position is quite straightforward. If public money is deliberately being channeled to gangs, then stop it. If an organization is being controlled by a gang and public money is being diverted for criminal benefit, then it needs to be dealt with.

But establish that through evidence. Target conduct, target control, target actual financial benefit. Do not allow association to become a substitute for evidence, and do not create a law so uncertain that legitimate Māori and community organizations working to reduce harm become collateral damage.

I'm asking the committee to either decline this bill in its current form or substantially amend it. Make the evidential threshold clear, make the meaning of indirectly clear, make the due diligence obligation clear, make it clear who can actually be criminally liable, and ensure legitimate Māori and community providers are not caught simply because of the people and communities they're working with.

Public money should not fund criminal organisations. I agree with that principle. But good legislation must do more than state a principle. It must establish the problem. It must respond proportionately to the evidence. It must be clear about who will carry the consequences when the law gets that distinction wrong. And for those reasons, I ask the committee not to recommend this bill in its current form.

Nga mihi. Thank you very much. I'm just looking to see if we've got any questions. I've got a question from Rima Nakley. Kia ora. Look, thank you for your submission. I read the written submission as well. I'm the member in charge of the bill, and as I've said to a number of other submitters, I hear your concern, particularly around the meaning of associated. And that's why I'm trying to make it clear, and hopefully I can make some changes where associated is not the word referred to. It's more affiliated.

And I hear you, that there's a lot of good organizations doing work with former gang members or people that are gang members that are trying to change their lifestyle. So thank you for sharing that, and I just want you to know that is on the forefront of my mind as we hope- Thank you... progress the bill. Thank- Nga mihi. Nga mihi. I have one. I've got one.

Stephen. Thanks, Lisa, and your points were all well-made. I just want to make sure, just in case I'm missing something, but what was ... The Indigenous Data Authority, is there a particular aspect to this bill that concerns the work you do, or am I missing something? So my organization actually works with Maori and indigenous organizations globally.

So obviously, being Maori myself and the thought of this impacting Maori organizations, et cetera, this is why we have put in a submission. That's your connection. Okay. I just want to make sure I wasn't missing a data point. Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Lisa. Really appreciate you joining us this afternoon- Thank you... and for your time.

Thank you. Appreciate it. Okay. We come to our next submitter, who is Craig Atkinson, who's also joining us on Zoom. Good afternoon, Craig. Thank you for joining us. We've got you down for five minutes, and we've read your written submission. Over to you. I'd sent an email through earlier, to do this in a private session. Is that possible or not?

No. This is a public session- Oh... and we take all submissions on the bill in public. Okey-dokey. That's fine. My first point is, well firstly, I'd like to say that I fully support what the previous submitter has just said, in every aspect of it. I would like to ask if there's ever been a royal inquiry into the formations of the gangs in New Zealand.

I know it's been spoke about, but if it's ever been put into a proper inquiry and why I say that is back in the early '90s, I met two patch members in England, and they were returning. They were both white males, and they'd left the British military.

And after leaving the British military, they got three offers, one to go to New Zealand, one to go to Northern Ireland, and to go to South Africa. And basically, the offer for New Zealand was to sit at the heads of the gangs. I'd say in my period while being in New Zealand, I've been targeted by one said gang.

And I would say that, yes, there was very much a connection there. That there wasn't just the younger sort of aspects, but the people that sit at the top of the gangs. I brought this up with a very close friend that was in the British military. And he took this up with his officer in command, and passed my details onto him. For the next three months, I received emails that were basically I was an ungrateful piece of s**t, and I should support the troops in whatever they did.

So I think there should be an inquiry into the formations of the gangs before we're sort of looking at that by the Crown. I realize the Crown wears many hats, whether it's in this country or other countries. But yeah, the formation and where gangs are used in British systems, I think, is unquestionable that you look at other countries that don't have the gang problems, and it is a part of the British system.

And it has been for many years. If you look at New Zealand 30 years ago, every small rural town and every city had one gang that were basically ... And then in later years, they've amalgamated, and grown. So yeah. That's where my point is with the formation of the gangs and ask for a full review into what the formations was and let people come forward and speak what their experiences have been.

Thank you, Craig. Doesn't appear we have any questions from members, so we're really grateful for your written submission and for joining us this afternoon. So thank you for your time. Kia ora. Thank you. Bye-bye. Okay, members, we now come to our final submitter, which is the member in charge of the bill, Rima Nakley. So I'm going to have Rima come up to the main table.

Hi. I'm sure this isn't necessary. Things like that. Thank you. Over to you, Rima. We've got 10 minutes, and- Thank you. Thank you... leave some time for questions. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Top angle. Okay. Look, I want to thank all the submitters before me that took the time to submit, and I think it was Associate Professor Carrick that's withdrawn from today, but I did read his submission as well.

And I'd just like to reiterate, in a nutshell, what this bill is about. And the Public Finance Prohibition on Providing Public Funds to Gangs Amendment bill is essentially about prohibiting the Crown from providing funds to organizations that are run directly or indirectly by gangs.

And I would like to recognize at this point, as I have with previous submitters, that the explanatory notes of the bill uses the word associated with gangs, and that's caused quite some concern, and rightfully so. And I've had the time to speak to a few community organizations that do excellent work in the field of rehabilitation and helping people rebuild their lives after being involved with drugs or gang membership that were concerned about the term associated because their work, they

are associated to gang members or to gangs by virtue of their work. And I want to make it really clear, and firstly I want to thank them for raising those concerns with me privately as well, and secondly, that it's a massive priority for me to make sure it's very clear that as we progress through this bill, and I hope it can get enough support across the House to progress it, that I don't want to capture association. And that's why in my first reading speech, I utilized the word affiliated as opposed to associated, because affiliation is a stronger,

more formal kind of concrete connection rather than an association. I'm associated to all of you through being in the same House of Parliament. So that's something I want to make it very clear, and I thank the people that also asked us to make indirectly clear.

We'll see how we can work through that. But there's no doubt about it in my mind that there is a current gap. And the current gap we saw being materialized, so to speak, in 2021 when $2.75 million of public funds- Mm-hmm... coming from the proceeds of crime, which put it under the umbrella of public funds, went to an association, or rather an organization, quite clearly affiliated with the Mongrel Mob. And even though that organization, some people may say the kaupapa was about rehabilitation, the sheer fact that they are connected to the Mongrel Mob,

and the Mongrel Mob currently engages in illegal criminal activity, a lot of which supplies drugs onto our streets. That, to me, and to everyone that was horrified by that decision, is a slap in the face, not to me, but to the families of victims, of people that are addicted to drugs or victims of criminal behavior at the hand of guns.

Pardon me, at the hand of gangs. And so for me, it's very simple. Mm-hmm. I don't want money that should be going to other organizations, public money that is, other organizations that do that hard and important work as well, to go to organizations that are affiliated to gangs. Because in a nutshell, as I have said before, those administering the poison should not be the one administering the antidote as well.

Mm. There's some questions with respect to how far does it go. I do want to raise, if you don't mind, a number of people have mentioned abuse in care at the hand of churches as well. And that is abhorrent, and that is, for me, those people that enacted that abuse and still do are despicable people. But however, members' bills are deliberately what we call the scope-... is specific, narrow. And so as much as those are very important suggestions and considerations with respect to this

member's bill, it's not going to fall under that. I'm sorry if that hurts some people, and I can understand the hurt. But the way that member's bills work is that they are specific and narrow. And that goes to family members of gangs as well, being given money through wins and things like that. That's been raised, and it's an actually a very legitimate question. But coming back to the narrow scope of members' bills, they won't fall under that.

There's a number of points I can raise, but I can see one of my colleagues, I think, has a question. So shall I leave it at that? But before I leave it at that, I do want to highlight that victims are at the center of this bill. And even though some people have said, "Where's the evidence?

What are you basing it on?" For me, when victims come first, it's very easy to understand that money, public money, should not be given to the people that have created these victims to a great extent. Mm. Thank you, Rima. Thank you, Mr. Chair. We have got a few questions. Start with Dr Laurence Yuen-Ahn.

Thank you, Chair. And thank you, Rima, for your presentation. Thank you. And I also want to thank the fact that you are really open to the idea of making changes to make it more- More specific in terms of what this is looking at. I just got, I guess, a couple of questions.

The affiliate and associate I think is a really important one, so I'm really pleased that you're looking into that. I wondered, is there any initiative I can think of currently, for example, in mental health, that potentially will be captured by this bill? Was that something maybe for us as a committee to look into, whether that'll be affected even if we use the term affiliated?

That being my first question. My second one is, have you thought about rather than specifically looking at gangs, but maybe looking at organized crime in general? Yeah. And the third one, and this is something that just occurred to me now. What happens if a member of parliament, through a democratic process, is elected, but someone who may have affiliations with gangs, are they going to be captured by this bill? I don't know.

Yep. Always the excellent questions from Dr. Lawrence. Would you like me to answer? Yeah, please. Thank you. With respect to the mental health situation, again, for me, it's very clear. If an organization is an organization affiliated to a gang, i.e., this organization was created by gang members, people that are proudly lifelong members of gangs that are still engaging in criminal activity and getting money from crime, then yep, that will be captured.

Mm. With respect to organized crime versus gangs, gangs are organized crime and we've got that list under, I think it is Section four, Section five of the Gangs Act. But I hear what you're saying. There could be times where organized crime hasn't yet been captured under that list, and when they're captured under that list, because the police are constantly doing their excellent work, I'm sure it will fall under.

But maybe if I can have more of a clearer, specific example, we can answer that more. Mm. And with respect to MP- Some questions... MPs having affiliations- I never questioned it, yeah... hopefully they're not from the Green Party. But no, joking. If they're affiliated, they're affiliated. So are you saying their pay being- Yeah. Is that a crown fund?

Yep. I hear what you're saying. I hear what you're saying. Maybe for us to look into. Yeah. It links to another question which we've had raised by other submitters is around gang members receiving the unemployment benefit or the job seeker benefit or a disability benefit or something like that, and whether, Rima, that is the intention behind your bill.

Yep. Do you want to just clarify the intent in that space? And so as I, going back to my initial remarks, I totally can understand, and I can see how that falls under that, and I was asked questions by reporters when this first was drawn. But in the spirit of the narrow scope of a member's bill, I don't think it would be wise for us to seriously consider that- Yeah, of course... under this member's bill.

Yeah. Something for the future. That makes sense. Well, it is something to think about. Thank you. Okay, question from Katie Nimon. Thanks, Rima. Thank you. The issue you talked about in specific is related to Hawke's Bay and sort of widely known. It's widely. Yes. And I think to your point, just to back up what you're saying, I think the test is pretty obvious, and so from what I'm hearing from the feedback and the questions around it is that to make it specifically government contracts- Mm.

Rather than- Yep... any kind of payment, is maybe a way of delineating. Mm. Yes. But the test, and I think that would be coming down to it, this is probably something more for advisors, but your interest, you have to be keen to see it happen to an extent. Is there being a test in that, is the contract to, in this particular case, the contract was to treat drug rehabilitation from drug addiction influenced or impacted by the sale of drugs from those same people and the association with those same people.

Mm. And so it then becomes the money go round, because it's coming from the proceeds of crime. So I think that becomes a really obvious test, and so my question is, do you have interest in there being a test that means some of this might fall outside the scope? Which means there could be some government money going to any kind of gang affiliated if it doesn't meet the test, but perhaps the test then becomes a bit stronger and stops inadvertent. There is an example of a loose affiliation where someone started a physical fitness that does

receive some MSD funding, and the association is quite loose, and the benefit is quite positive, and so perhaps there's a test that allows there to be a bit of a- Yep... a line. That's a probing concept. Thank you, Katie Nimon. And one final question from Camilla Belich.

But just want to say, Mr. Chair, if you don't mind, that I'd like our officials to also please note that down. Yeah. Whether we can incorporate that without going outside the narrow scope. Yep. Thank you. Camilla. Yes. Thanks. And I think that's a really good suggestion. And an example that might be covered by that was the $30,000 that 2017 went to Hard to Reach. Is that the kind of contract that would be covered by this type of proposal that Katie's suggesting, like a government funding through the Ministry of Social Development to a organization that has an

affiliation with a gang member? And if I recall correctly, Kahukura does come under the umbrella of Hard to Reach. That's my recollection. But yep, these are good questions that I hope we consider, and I particularly want our good people that are doing great work around the country to be reassured that these are questions that we're considering.

Thank you, colleagues. Mr. Chair, is there any more time? No, that's it, I'm sorry. Well, you're a great chair. Thanks, everyone. Thank you very much, Rima. Thank you. Thank you. Well done. Well done. Okay, members, that concludes our hearings on this bill. We'll just move out of public session.
